record.original_question: Does every polygon admit at least one periodic billiard orbit?

evidence.quote: Problem 10. Does every polygon have a periodic orbit?
It is not known if every acute triangle has other periodic orbits; it is also not known if every obtuse triangle has a periodic orbit.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A billiard trajectory in a polygon $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is the trajectory of a point particle moving in straight lines inside $P$ and reflecting off the boundary according to the law of equal angles (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection); trajectories that hit a vertex are considered undefined at that point. Such a trajectory is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Question: Does every polygon $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ (i.e. every simply connected planar region bounded by finitely many line segments) admit at least one periodic billiard trajectory?
artifact.status_search_result: The general question remains open. Known partial results: Fagnano (1775) gave a periodic orbit in every acute triangle; Masur (1986) established existence of periodic orbits in every rational polygon (all angles rational multiples of π); Holt (1993) handled right triangles; and Schwartz proved existence for every obtuse triangle whose angles are all at most 100°. The case of general (irrational) polygons, and even general obtuse triangles, is still unresolved.

status_evidence.title: The Mysterious Math of Billiards Tables | Quanta Magazine
status_evidence.snippet: Masur used this technique to show that all polygonal tables with rational angles have periodic orbits... whether every obtuse triangle has a periodic orbit remains open.
status_evidence.claim: Existence is known for rational polygons but unknown for general polygons including general obtuse triangles.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Triangular Billiards I: Near the (2,3,6) Triangle
status_evidence.snippet: Schwartz's program establishing periodic orbits for obtuse triangles with angles bounded above by 100 degrees.
status_evidence.claim: Schwartz proved existence of periodic orbits for obtuse triangles with all angles at most 100°.

status_evidence.title: On Periodic Billiard Trajectories in Obtuse Triangles
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses partial results on existence of periodic billiard orbits in obtuse triangles.
status_evidence.claim: The obtuse-triangle case has only partial results.
